source.title: Why Do Large Language Models Generate Harmful Content?

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some plot labels are garbled by text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses causal activation replacement and measures changes in harmful-versus-harmless output distributions, a different approach to causal mediation. It does not test the specific difference-in-means direction.
record.gate_note: The study intervenes on model layers, blocks, neuron blocks, and prompt-token activations, but does not find or ablate the claimed single direction, add it, or measure refusal/compliance rates or general capability. Its reported IE is an L1 distance between output distributions. Rows therefore describe related causal-mediation results as versions ["none"]. The late-layer steering defense's roughly 4% improvement is the study's own new method, not a test of the claimed direction, and is not recorded as a row for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study cites the original (ref. [2]) only in related work. It never derives, ablates or adds a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. It patches whole layers, MLP and attention outputs, neuron blocks and token positions with harmless-run activations. Its measure is a change in the L1 distance between next-token distributions, not a refusal or compliance rate, and it runs no capability check. Per the gate, a related but different construct with no refusal rate does not test any version, so its findings go under fits_no_version. The record's 'tests/T2' guess is not supported: every row is already linked to 'none'. The late-layer steering defense is the authors' own method. Its vector construction is unspecified, and it is reported only as a roughly 4% defense gain.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with additions. The authors conclude that late-layer MLP blocks generate the harmful or refusal signal, early attention provides contextual processing of harmfulness, and a sparse set of final-layer neurons gates generation. They also find causal weight concentrated in the final prompt-token group. They recommend targeted interventions on late MLP components over broad fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses causal mediation with harmful/harmless activation replacement at layer, module, neuron-block, and token levels; measures output-distribution L1-distance change rather than deriving and ablating a single difference-in-means direction.
record.method_sensitivity: IE varies by layer and component: late layers and late MLP blocks are positive, middle layers are near zero, and the final layer is negative; token-group IE is highest for the final prompt quartile. The text also reports different IE magnitudes for base and instruction-tuned variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying a steering vector toward a 'harmless' latent representation at the K=3 highest-IE late layers improves defense against modified AdvBench harmful prompts by about 4% (LLM judge, Fig. 7). No detailed numbers or uncertainty are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-stream steering at late layers selected by causal-mediation IE modestly increases refusal of harmful prompts.

record.problems: The reported IE measures output-distribution divergence rather than refusal or compliance rates. The neuron analysis uses contiguous hidden-dimension blocks and explicitly assumes related neurons are spatially adjacent; most models show no statistically significant neuron-level peak. Many model- and layer-specific values are presented in plots rather than described numerically in the text. The late-layer steering defense's roughly 4% result is stated without detailed numbers or uncertainty in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The study contains many per-layer and per-component heatmap cells, token-wise plots, and a top-token flip-rate plot. Their individual values are not reported in the text, and the catalog keeps the text-described aggregate patterns and the captioned late-MLP values rather than transcribing all figure cells. The late-layer steering defense comparison and its roughly 4% improvement are not recorded as claim-version rows because this is the study's own new steering method, not the claimed direction.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is found, ablated or added. There is no refusal or compliance rate and no capability retention check.
No jailbreak-suppression or adversarial-ablation training tested.
No affine, cone or multi-direction analysis.
Harmfulness judgment and refusal are not measured separately.
No transfer of a direction across languages or models. Base and instruct models are compared only by IE magnitude.
Base vs instruct IE magnitudes are noted, but not whether training creates a removable direction.

record.verdict_notes: The IE measure is a next-token L1 divergence on minimal-pair prompts, so it cannot show refusal removal or induction. The neuron-level analysis was non-significant for most models, yet the authors still call it sparse mediation. The top-token case study (Table 1) is a single prompt pair.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not identify a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, project it out at every layer and position, add it to induce refusals to harmless requests, or assess whether general capability is retained. Its output-distribution IE measure does not directly report refusal or compliance.
No weight-edit ablation or released-model abliteration is tested.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction representation of refusal is measured or compared.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decisions.
No cross-language transfer or transfer of the claimed direction between base and instruct models is tested.
Base and instruction-tuned models are compared, but the study does not test when or how refusal training creates a removable direction.
